commenti.body: No I think that misses the point of what the movie is trying to say. It’s better to show the consequences of having never been born, which ultimately saves George’s life because he realizes how many other lives he’s affected.

There’s a logic to what you’re saying, although in truth it wouldn’t be so different. Many of the bad things would have been the same. But the way it is in the film is much more impactful emotionally, and ultimately that’s more important for a Capra movie and its message.

Also, that message is more than just “being selfless ultimately pays off”. It’s also “pull on all the threads of a life and so much falls apart”. That’s about more than just George’s choices (although those are also important), it’s about how wonderful the impact of the whole tapestry of a life can be.

No because then the message of the movie would have been, "Don't follow your dreams or everyone you care about will suffer horribly, and the world will be a worse place," and that would have been a terrible message.

No, that misses the point of the movie. It wouldn’t make George appreciate the life he has now. George was suicidal because after a life where he has to sacrifice many dreams and make many concessions due to obligation, he still ended up in a situation where he was financially screwed and facing jailtime. If the path where he traveled the world and went to college was also bad, that wouldn’t help George now. He would just think “it was going to be bad no matter what” which honestly would reinforce his negative thoughts that the world would be better off without them. To find value in his current life, he needed to see the tangible way in which he made a positive impact. It doesn’t matter if a world where he went to college and traveled is better or worse, what matters is that George has a life worth appreciating regardless.

It's a good thought experiment. I agree with the other responses that it sort of missed the point of the movie to show him living out his dream, but what if (like many people) the dream is never what they actually think it is? What if he does go away from Bedford Falls, lives in the big city, initially is swindled due to his small-town good nature, but then eventually becomes hardened like another Mr. Potter and achieved success as a wealthy banker? Then he realizes how miserable he is, comes home for nostalgic reasons, and then sees how similar to Mr. Potter he's become, and how everything he loved in life is now lost.

It would be kind of like an American Cinema Paradiso. I think it could work, but the message would essentially be the same as the current movie, unless you're going in a completely different direction.

Well…no. Because George is the one who’s trying to enact an action, his suicide, and then an acceleration into his own nonexistence. At that point of the story, George feels like a burden, he’s not so much lamenting the loss of his aspirations, but that he’s screwed everyone in the town. It would, at best, mean nothing to him to see how happy he could have been, on his own, and at worst, you can assume a similar outcome for the town, minus his brother’s death as a child.

In a broader, thematic sense, George had a wonderful life, so to show an idyllic version of his life where he leaves the town wouldn’t really make sense and would be a waste of time that undercuts the point.

That’s true and I think the movie works best how it is, we don’t need to see how it would’ve played out. But I do think there’s something to be said that the movie does show that doing the right thing for your community sometimes requires something of us, including a few dreams. 

He’d have his hearing, gone to the college he wanted to go to, saw the world, and made lots of money. I think it could be said that one of the points is that there’s something richer to be found in life when you, at least to an extent, put others/the community first over individualism. Especially with the “No man is a failure who has friends.”. The movie already shows this though and wouldn’t make sense for the angel to show how exciting all his dreams would’ve been.

I agree with many of the other posters. However, I think it would have been interesting to show that the parallel life that wasn't lived had flavors of the same struggles and doubts that George was facing in his real life. 

Making me realize that this and EEAAO could be an interesting double feature.

Man, as much as I adore the original arc of George Bailey's journey, I gotta say - your idea to switch up Clarence's role hears a pretty damn fascinating bell! Kind of a "careful what you wish for" twist. But thinking about it, there's a fundamental melancholy about George's unfulfilled wanderlust, which, while it might have been interesting to explore, could potentially derail the film's heartfelt focus on small-town life and the value of the 'ordinary' man. But wow, that really does pose a one-of-a-kind perspective. Interesting stuff, my dude!

I'd wondered for decades why people watched something as harrowing as *Life is Beautiful* every year around Christmastime. 
Then, recently, we watched *It's a Wonderful Life* and I realized my mix-up.
